title: Submissions by the Defence & Prosecution, completion of Cross-examination (Day 10), Re-examination by Ben Myers KC
section: Lucy Letby - Final day of Cross-examination & Re-examination by Ben Myers KC

blocks.text: 9 June 2023
Applications by the Defence Lucy Letby - Cross-examination Day 9: Events following the alleged offences and other matters
Re-examination by Ben Myers KC
CONTENTS
Applications Submissions by MR MYERS and MR JOHNSON
MS LUCY LETBY (continued)
Cross-examination by MR JOHNSON (continued)
Re-examination by MR MYERS
Housekeeping
Friday, 9 June 2023
(In the absence of the jury)
Applications

Mr Johnson, Mr Myers, there are two issues now we have to address. Perhaps we could deal with what I perceive to be the shorter one, which is the matter that Mr Johnson raised about the interruption of his cross-examination at that particular point. I have seen what you have written, Mr Johnson. Essentially, you're seeking clarification as to whether it was a false point.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Not deliberately a false point --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, no.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: -- but a false point by reason of circumstances or not.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Mr Myers.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Submissions by MR MYERS
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: One moment, please, my Lord, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The issue that arises, or arose, in the course of crossexamination -- I'm grateful for a copy of the transcript we have here -- arose as two things were unfolding so far as our
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: concerns were engaged. The first was the extent to which the
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: cross-examination was heading towards, however that happened,
issues of privilege.
Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That was a real concern. And the second was our concern that the defendant not be at any disadvantage as to what her case should be.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: As to whether this is something that needs to be dealt with in the way suggested by the prosecution before the jury, we say that is unnecessary and inappropriate. But I'll deal with the situation to explain the position that we're in.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Plainly, that evidence is agreed. That's how it's gone before the jury. Now, the defendant's position from her defence statement, which we haven't looked at, is at paragraph 163, was that in general:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "I cannot recall what conversations I had with [Baby N]'s parents, but I did not call his father to tell him about [Baby N]. The nursing notes say that Bernadette Butterworth contacted the persons."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Is there an issue, therefore? Well, it is apparent that there is an issue and therefore should it have been agreed in that circumstance? No. That's how that appears from that. And to have done so is a mistake.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Ultimately, that will rest with me.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Now, it's important in identifying that, that I also identify this. The way in which this point has developed in crossexamination is something that we were unaware of, and I'll come to what I mean by this, before we ever embarked upon the defendant's cross-examination, and that is the suggestion that Bernadette Butterworth is a fictitious entry in the notes. That isn't anything that we were aware was part of this case, as far as I can recall, until the defendant came to be cross-examined.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: If it was the case that this from the outset had been revealed as an assault in that way on that issue, it's difficult to see how it wouldn't have the prominence to engage a direct challenge. I'm saying this because of the suggestion this be rehearsed before the jury.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The purpose of having notification of the prosecution case is that we know the extent and nature of what we're dealing with. The prominence of this and the questioning about putting a lie in the notes about Bernadette Butterworth was news to us.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: She's been a witness in this case. If this is the prosecution position, that's something that properly should have been dealt with with a statement from her in some way or dealing with it with her. She's been available throughout, there have been many statements taken, and she's attended to give evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I point this out to make it plain that whilst I acknowledge, in light of the defence statement, that agreed evidence of this type is or may be a mistake, that's happened in circumstances where the nature of what is being said is completely unclear until cross-examination and the prominence of that nursing note and what is said about it not clear at all.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: All right. Thank you. I understand what you're saying. I'm not stopping you for a reason that is adverse to you. I'm actually just going to seek clarification. Mr Johnson, are you going to seek to pursue this point?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Submissions by MR JOHNSON
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: About the Bernie Butterworth note? Absolutely.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You can make the point, but Mr Myers has said it shouldn't have been agreed, this statement.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Well --
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's what it's all about, whether she is making that point up when she's giving her evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Well, this is all part of a larger issue.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, it is, but you've got many other examples, if I may say so.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Oh yes. Yes. Yes, absolutely. But, with respect, Mr Myers needs to make it clear to the jury that the fault lies with him.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think that's what he's going to do.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That's fine. I have absolutely no problem.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: What I want to avoid, and that's why I put in my note this morning:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Out of justice to the defendant this needs to be clarified."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Because the impression the jury may have is that I was doing something wrong and I wasn't.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I understand that. That's why Mr Myers has said that --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: -- but I don't think we need to go into the details of it.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, no.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Just say that Mr Myers accepts that on the instructions that he had, that should not have been agreed.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, that's fine.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I should say it's our concern as to the justice of this that led me to get to my feet when I did to make the objection that I did.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That's why I stopped it at that point because I'm familiar with this sort of situation -- and there is so much detail in this case in any event.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Further submissions by MR MYERS
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm grateful for that, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: There we are.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We can say, yes, that is something -- that is a mistake in agreeing that, we can see that, and I'll also deal with that in due course in one way or another.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I'm guided by your Lordship. Our observations on the point about Bernadette Butterworth are part of what we say about the way this point has developed. I don't want to go beyond what your Lordship regards appropriate to say at this point. If it's simply a case of saying that the defendant's case was that she didn't call him, it's also that the nursing notes say Bernie Butterworth contacted the parents, that is what she says, but if what's required is to say that statement should not have been agreed, I can say that and that's a mistake, and not of the defendant's, in terms of agreeing it.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Further submissions by MR JOHNSON
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And make it clear, with respect, that the line taken in cross-examination was reasonable.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That there's no criticism of the questions, the problem arose because a mistake was made by the defence, not a fault of the prosecution.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can I just deal with the Bernadette Butterworth point as well, please, my Lord?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: There is clear evidence from the parents that the person who made the call was Lucy Letby. The idea that the prosecution then have to scoot off to --
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I'm with you on that point. It's not something --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: And that should not be said in a speech either because it's implying fault in the prosecution.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I disagree with that firmly.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Look, I'm going to put this to bed at the moment because we've got other things to be getting on with. There needs to be resolution between the two of you as to what is going to be said to the jury, in agreed form, and if you can't agree it then you can make your respective submissions as to what should be said and I will say how it should be dealt with. All right?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Very well, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I appreciate it is a point and it's a point that needs to be addressed but it can be addressed, to my mind, relatively straightforwardly, accommodating both sides' positions.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Very well, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Can we move on to perhaps the more significant issue? I'm very grateful to both sides for providing me with the written material. Can I just say that I see this issue as being an issue that was addressed in the case of Grocott.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, this is 8-347 of Archbold.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. It appears in 4-407 in Archbold.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's referring to the case of Scott and then the more recent -it was Lord Justice Toulson who gave the judgment of the Court of Appeal. Again, I think we need to be clear about precisely what it is you are seeking to do --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: -- then we can take it from there.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I understand why the schedule has been drawn up because otherwise it would be very difficult.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Exactly.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: But before we come on to the use of the schedule, let's decide what it is you are wanting to put.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It is basically to put to the witness the fact that there is a body of material, I won't describe the nature of that material, but a body of material which tends to undermine evidence that she gave about her circumstances following her removal from the unit.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Precisely.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Exactly. Now, I'm going to address that first as an issue in this case. Mr Myers, is there any basis for objecting to that being done?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'd like to --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: In other words, putting to the witness in
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: cross-examination that there is material which may, depending on
the view taken by the jury of it, undermine evidence that she's given about a particular issue.
Further submissions by MR MYERS
It's difficult to answer that anyway from where we are than to say that the defence view is that the material doesn't undermine what she said.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Ah well, that's going to cause you difficulty then, because this is -- the principle is clear from 4-407:
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "That the judge has a discretion to admit evidence in rebuttal in situations other than contemplated in Frost above has been stated in these courts."
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's limited by the principle that:
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "Evidence which is clearly relevant, not marginally, minimally or doubtfully relevant, to the issues and within the prosecution and the Crown should be adduced by the prosecution as part of their case."
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Are you saying this should have been adduced by the prosecution as part of their case?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Well, no, we have raised four points and relevance is of one of them. And the point we make with relevance most precisely is that this doesn't go to do, we say, what the prosecution says it does, which is to negate some false impression that they maintain has been created. We don't accept that this material goes to show that she was necessarily anything other than in the state that she says she was in over the relevant period.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, that's then for the...
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The first step, though, at this stage of the proceedings must surely be whether the prosecution are entitled to rely upon that, given where we've got to.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The question in the first instance, putting aside the points and the concerns we raise as to our ability to consider the nature of the material that's been produced, is as to whether the relevance arises ex improviso.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We've identified four grounds on which we object to it: the nature of the material; whether the relevance does arise ex improviso, we say it doesn't; whether it's relevant anyway; and whether there's any unfairness.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Can we deal whether it arises ex improviso?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: You have just said that it's not material that the prosecution should have adduced as part of their case. You would have objected to it, I have no doubt.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, because we'd say it's not relevant. But in any event before we get to that point, the reason that they say -even if we're wrong about that, let me put it that way, and the material is prima facie relevant, the reason they seek to introduce it now rather than dealing with it during the defence case is that they say that the defendant's evidence engages this and it's something that arises for the first time, couldn't have been foreseen, and therefore they are now entitled to put it in. Because if this could have been foreseen during the prosecution case, it should have been introduced and we should have been having this argument then, not now.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The suggestion that Ms Letby's case is that she was in a state of mental turmoil, unwell, feeling isolated, unable to contact other people, isn't something that was made for the first time in evidence-in-chief. It was identified clearly beforehand, not least by virtue of the fact that we were required to set out a document explaining the relevance of material. And I put it in two annexes to our argument: what we said about that on 24 April with regard to the evidence of Eirian Powell, and the prosecution's response, in which they incorporate what we've said about Ms Letby and her increasing isolation and unhappiness.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So this isn't a new issue. If at that point the prosecution were of the view, ah well, this goes to bear upon that, they had every chance to do so. That, I respectfully observe, is the whole purpose of this.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And that's why, in my respectful submission, the first question is: has this genuinely arisen ex improviso?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And we say that it hasn't, relevant or not.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: All right. Mr Johnson?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Further submissions by MR JOHNSON
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: This material didn't go to an issue in the case before the defendant introduced this as an issue, so it was inadmissible before the defendant gave evidence in the terms she did. She has set this hare running.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We are entitled to shoot it if we can.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: (Pause)
Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: A simple point.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Further submissions by MR MYERS
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, my Lord, all I can say in response to that is we were specifically asked to identify issues for relevance and we've listed, on 24 April, that Eirian Powell's evidence is relevant to Lucy Letby's circumstances post-removal from the unit, her increasing isolation and unhappiness. That couldn't be -- that was done directly in response to a request from the prosecution and your Lordship in light of the prosecution's concerns to identify the issues to which this went. There couldn't be a better illustration of the fact it was identified, and Ms Powell was questioned accordingly.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Further submissions by MR JOHNSON
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: My Lord, I can raise another point in answer to that. The defendant's case has changed between that document and her evidence. What she said -- well, what was being suggested when Eirian Powell was giving evidence was that she was told she couldn't talk about the circumstances of her suspension from the unit. What she has said in the witness box is she was forbidden from communicating with people from the NNU and that cut her off from her family. That's the point. That's why what was irrelevant has become relevant.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: (Pause)
Right. Yes, Mr Myers.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Further submissions by MR MYERS
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We've dealt with that in paragraph 4 -- in fact, there was cross-examination on that very issue with Eirian Powell. I don't propose just to repeat what your Lordship has in writing from us. In fact, the witness was then cross-examined about impact from the removal and limited contact with other people.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: What the prosecution are saying is: yes, that was something that was raised, but she has gone considerably further than what was being considered relevant at that time. She has made specific assertions, which are set out in the prosecution note.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: And they're saying that that creates a false impression.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Well, ultimately, questions of rebuttal evidence and its introduction will lie with your Lordship's discretion on it.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It is a matter for discretion.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It is a matter for discretion.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It goes both to whether it is permissible at all -- admissible at all, sorry, I meant to say, admissible at all, and, if it is admissible, the form in which it should be admitted.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'll say this -- and I hope it's in order to assist: I would be -- it is proposed, is it, Mr Johnson, that the jury have a copy of this schedule to keep and not to use as a document to be referred to during the course of any permitted questioning in relation to it?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Further submissions by MR JOHNSON
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: What we were proposing to do -- we have it available digitally for deployment on the screens.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We weren't proposing to give the jury a paper copy.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I am pleased to hear that because that would be inappropriate.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We respectfully agree. It all depends on the answers that we get, of course, how much detail we have to go into.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, exactly, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: If the defendant decides that actually she wasn't telling the truth to the jury about all this then very quickly we can dispose of it. If she persists in the line that she has adopted then it would involve a more granular approach. That's out of my control.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: All right. Mr Myers, then the starting point is that if I permit the prosecution to ask questions in relation to the material that's set out on the schedule, the jury will not have a paper copy. Any particular piece of material that the prosecution wish to ask the defendant about will be put up on the screen, as I understand it, as an isolated piece of material; is that right, Mr Johnson?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. The schedule as it appears in writing or as it appears in the printed copy is rather more manageable as a digital document, it's more legible.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that can be done that way.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The purpose of giving it in paper to the defendant is so that she can look at context.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Exactly.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Because as we've seen on many occasions with these documents, context is important. So if she wants to make any points, she can do.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That leads me on to the next question: whether she should be provided with a paper copy --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Absolutely.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: -- she should have a paper copy and the opportunity to -- and an opportunity to consider it before she resumes her evidence?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I have absolutely no objection to that at all.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Further submissions by MR MYERS
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We have no observations as to that, but one matter I do identify, my Lord, and it's something we make reference to in our note prepared in the short compass of time available, is that as the prosecution well know, the defendant's mental state has marked fragilities associated with, amongst other things, the impact of matters relating to times at the arrest and also, we submit, affected by things from this period.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It won't be unknown to the prosecution the likely consequence of putting this material before her. They see a gain in that and have made an application -- a forensic gain and they have made an application to the court under this note to use this material. One of the concerns that we list under unfairness, along with its potential prejudicial impact when set against the allegations, is its potential to cause upset or destabilisation for what we submit is, at best, relatively little gain.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, it's not for you to -- you can submit that, but that's not a --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Very well. I do say simply because we have a genuine concern as to its impact, I won't enlarge upon that because your Lordship has the material. But the business of showing it to the defendant, going through it with the defendant, we shall see how that proceeds.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Exactly.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It causes us significant concern.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It may be the case. Mr Johnson, is there anything else you wish to say at this stage?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Further submissions by MR JOHNSON
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No. If it helps Mr Myers, I was planning to deal with this material at the end of the list of matters that I'm dealing with today, so if it has the effect he fears then it won't prevent me from having asked other questions.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Now, the issue then, and this is a matter for my learned friend's judgement, I am happy for the defendant to be given advance notice of this. If my learned friend thinks it's helpful
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: for her to have it now, I am happy. If he thinks she shouldn't be given it now, I am happy.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It would be more helpful to have it sooner than later.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Fine, let's do that then.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: She should be provided with a coloured copy because it's so much easier than a black and white one --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's here.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: -- and afforded an opportunity to look at it.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I think she may need a bit of time to get to grips with what it shows. I'll leave that for your Lordship and my learned friend to judge how much.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I would think -- well, it's material of which she will be aware because it's come from her mobile phone and other -- is it all from her mobile phone and some paper documents?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Diary, Facebook, mobile phone.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: How long, Mr Myers?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thirty minutes, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I was going to say 20 to 30 minutes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I should say, before we conclude this, that I'm grateful to Mr Maher and Ms Clancy, who were up until the small hours trying to make what they could of such material as we have had. Your Lordship has seen our observation that are in excess of 150,000 pages of material, not all of which we understand we have. But they have done their best to deal with it.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: One matter we raised was the difficulty of dealing with it in the time available. I don't raise that now because we know how we're proceeding, but I think on their behalf I would like to acknowledge the work they did, extensive work, in assisting me in dealing with this application.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The court is very grateful to you and them. So what we will do is we will rise now. I will set out my reasons for my ruling in writing in due course, but I just wanted to make progress with the trial at this stage and why I'm
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: exercising my discretion as I am. So a copy can be provided to the defendant now. She is being given a copy.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Just so that you understand, this is a schedule that's been prepared, Ms Letby, of material that you've heard is downloads from your phone, from your Facebook page -- I think it's a Facebook page, isn't it, or pages?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm not the person to ask, my Lord, I'm sorry.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And I'm not. And from diaries. It's all in chronological order and the reason you're being given this now is so you can familiarise yourself with it because you'll be asked some questions about it. This document is not going to go before the jury as a document, but it may be, depending on what you say about the contents of this document, there may be sections that are put up on the screen? All right? So that's the process that's going to be undertaken.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you. We'll say we'll sit again at 10.55.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (A short break)
My Lord, before we begin, shall I just confirm the issue of the mistake? If I make that plain, that is my mistake that that statement was agreed.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That's what I understand the prosecution wish, with your Lordship's leave.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: No, we also ask for my learned friend to make it clear that my line of questioning was unobjectionable.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I make it clear to this extent: exploring the issue is unobjectionable; the manner of questioning we do not accept is unobjectionable. That's something I cannot accept. But at this point we can say that it's a legitimate line of questioning to have explored that with the defendant.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, let me make a note then. If I was to say to the jury that the defence acknowledge -- well, I'm wondering whether... You acknowledge that it was a mistake to agree the evidence --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Can I invite your Lordship to put it in context to this degree --
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: part of the summing-up, which, as I have said to you from the outset of this trial, will be a rehearsal of the events, not in minute detail, but going through each event and the evidence that you've heard and the nature of the evidence and providing you with references to some of the main features of it. blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So a long weekend for you, obviously, now. All right?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much. Wednesday morning, 10.30.
